items.title: Les interdictions de sortie du territoire ont explosé depuis l’arrivée au pouvoir de Xi Jinping
items.description: La base de données de la Cour populaire suprême chinoise (最高人民法院) a enregistré près de 200 000 occurrences du terme « 限制出境 », soit l'interdiction de sortie du territoire, pour la seule année 2025. Ces mentions ont ainsi été multipliées par plus de 4 300 depuis 2014, selon les données compilées par Safeguard Defenders, soit l'année qui a suivi l'arrivée au pouvoir de Xi Jinping, en mars 2013 Shutdown : China’s rapid expansion of exit bans , Safeguard Defenders, 15 septembre 2026.'> 1 . Le dirigeant chinois a plus que doublé le corpus juridique permettant de prononcer des interdictions de sortie du territoire visant des citoyens chinois ou des étrangers. La Chine compte ainsi 18 lois et instruments susceptibles d’être utilisés pour prononcer des interdictions de sortie du territoire. Plusieurs analystes considèrent que la dernière de ces régulations, publiée le 31 juillet par le Conseil d’État et entrée en vigueur hier, mardi 15 septembre, « ramène la Chine à l'interdiction des voyages à l'étranger qui prévalait sous le régime de Mao » China tightens control of overseas travel in sweeping new law », Financial Times , 15 septembre 2026.'> 2 . Ces nouvelles dispositions élargissent les circonstances dans lesquelles les citoyens chinois peuvent être interdits de quitter le territoire, notamment en cas d’infractions liées au contrôle des exportations et aux technologies China's new exit and entry regulation : What multinational companies need to know , DLA Piper, 4 août 2026.'> 3 . L’article 4 du texte prévoit ainsi une interdiction de sortie du territoire d’une durée allant de six mois à trois ans pour un ressortissant chinois qui se serait livré à l’étranger « à des activités illégales ou criminelles mettant en danger la sécurité ou les intérêts nationaux ». Les règles s’appliqueraient aussi bien aux fonctionnaires, aux cadres du Parti et aux employés des entreprises publiques qu’aux particuliers travaillant dans des secteurs considérés « sensibles » par Pékin. Ce durcissement intervient dans le cadre d’une course technologique de plus en plus intense avec les États-Unis. En mars, le régime chinois avait interdit aux dirigeants de la start-up d’IA Manus, dont le PDG et cofondateur Xiao Hong, de quitter le pays pendant que les autorités étudiaient l’acquisition de l’entreprise par Meta. La Commission nationale du développement et de la réforme avait finalement ordonné, en avril, le retrait de l'offre, au nom de la sécurité nationale et de la protection des actifs technologiques. L’article Les interdictions de sortie du territoire ont explosé depuis l’arrivée au pouvoir de Xi Jinping est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .

Imran’s sisters, lawyers denied meeting at Adiala
items.description: • Aleema says KP should not accord protocol to Nawaz during his visits to province • PTI information secretary rejects FCC’s decision to seek SC record on ex-PM’s proposed hospital transfer ISLAMABAD:While Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) Chief Minister Sohail Afridi has been facing a “tough time” in Lahore , Imran Khan’s sister Aleema Khan on Tuesday suggested that protocol should not be accorded to former prime minister Nawaz Sharif during his visits to KP. She was speaking to media persons outside Adiala jail after, once again, she was not allowed to meet her brother in violation of the Isla­mabad High Court’s (IHC) orders. Advocate Awais Younas Chau­dhry, who submits lists of leaders and lawyers to the jail administration seeking permission to meet Imran Khan, told Dawn that his sisters and six lawyers reached outside Adiala jail but were not allowed to meet the PTI founder. “The sisters waited there even after 6:30pm, but they were not informed about the approval of the meeting. The IHC has ordered that meetings of the family and lawyers with Imran Khan be arranged on Tuesdays and meetings of party leaders on Thursdays, but the court orders are being violated,” he said. Ms Khan, while talking to media persons, claimed that the ruling elite was scared and was preparing to flee the country. When asked about the IHC’s orders that roads should not be blocked during protests, she said: “You will see that the government will itself close the roads. After that, IHC Chief Justice Sardar Muhammad Sarfraz Dogar should call the government and ask it to open the roads,” she suggested. Replying to a question, Ms Khan said she would suggest that Justice Sarfraz Dogar summon her if she was committing contempt of court. Another sister of Imran Khan, Dr Uzma Khan, said the judges had insulted the whole country, but the media was asking whether the sisters had disgraced the judiciary. Replying to a question, Aleema Khan said the constitutional court had been established unconstitutionally. “We were not aware of their names, but due to social media, now we know them very well. Justice Baqar Najafi sent Nawaz Sharif abroad on a Rs50 stamp paper and forgot to ask why he was not returning. Now he has been worrying that Imran Khan should not come out of jail,” she added. She said the constitutional court had been established to undermine the Supreme Court (SC) and that its aim was to keep Imran Khan in jail. “It is necessary for the SC to ensure its survival and integrity,” she suggested. She said she had suggested to Sohail Afridi that he make two demands: first, that Imran Khan be shifted to Shifa International Hospital, as those who had put him in jail were allegedly involved in attempts to kill him; and second, that Justice Dogar should start hearing Imran Khan’s bail applications. When asked about the KP chief minister having a “tough time” in Lahore, she said that, in response, the KP government should not accord protocol to Nawaz Sharif during his visits to the province. FCC decision Meanwhile, PTI Central Infor­m­ation Secretary Sheikh Waqas Akram rejected the Federal Cons­titutional Court’s (FCC) decision to summon from the SC the record of the case concerning PTI founder Imran Khan’s transfer to a hospital, calling the move a blatant manifestation of how the top court had been deliberately weakened and rendered virtually ineffective throu­gh the 26th and 27th Constitutional Amendments. Mr Akram urged the FCC to exercise the utmost restraint and refrain from interfering in matters already pending before the SC, the country’s apex judicial forum. Published in Dawn, September 16th, 2026

items.title: L’armée américaine ne sait plus faire la guerre
items.description: Pour préparer votre rentrée, testez le Grand Continent . Les idées et les analyses qu’on ne trouve nulle part. Mais que vous verrez bientôt partout. Dans votre boîte mail à partir de 8 euros par mois Tout a commencé avec la stratégie du « shock and awe », choc et effroi , qui a accompagné presque toutes les guerres majeures menées par les États-Unis au cours du dernier demi-siècle, et qui a récemment été illustrée par le conflit contre l'Iran. La démonstration écrasante de force lors de l’attaque initiale menée conjointement par les États-Unis et Israël contre des cibles iraniennes, marquée par les images familières de frappes de précision, de forces ennemies paralysées et de civils sous le choc, a été amplifiée par l’élimination d’une grande partie de l'élite dirigeante, dont le Guide suprême, l’ayatollah Ali Khamenei. Même si cette attaque a été menée par l’armée de l’air israélienne, l’assaut implacable des forces américaines contre des cibles militaires et des positions de la Garde révolutionnaire a semblé confirmer la position hégémonique incontestée des États-Unis sur le plan militaire. Six mois plus tard, la situation est bien différente. La guerre que le président Donald Trump espérait voir durer quelques jours, quelques semaines seulement est toujours en cours, sans qu'une issue politique claire se profile. L’Iran a démontré sa capacité à perturber le trafic maritime dans le détroit d'Ormuz et à menacer les bases américaines et leurs alliés dans la région. Les stocks de défense aérienne et antimissile sont sous pression et les navires et avions sont mobilisés depuis bien plus longtemps que prévu. Des dizaines de milliers de soldats américains restent déployés et les missions sont prolongées jusqu’en 2027, malgré les avertissements des hauts gradés concernant les conséquences sur les autres théâtres d'opérations. L’escale de l’USS Abraham Lincoln à Pattaya, en Thaïlande, après 286 jours de présence en mer, avec un équipage épuisé et une coque rouillée, offre une métaphore inconfortable pour un establishment militaire qui reste immensément puissant, mais à qui l’on demande d’en faire plus que ne le permettent ses fondements institutionnels. Il est tentant d'attribuer les causes de cette crise aux décisions erratiques de la deuxième administration Trump et aux perturbations infligées au corps des officiers par le secrétaire à la Guerre, Pete Hegseth . Pourtant, l’état de plus en plus précaire de l’armée américaine ne saurait se réduire aux événements des deux dernières années. Ses origines remontent au « dividende de la paix » du début des années 1990, en passant par les dysfonctionnements causés par la guerre contre le terrorisme après 2001, jusqu'à la réticence, durant les années 2010, à remettre en question les hypothèses fondamentales concernant les acquisitions, la logistique, la doctrine, le rôle des alliés et la nature même de la puissance militaire. Trump et Hegseth sont donc autant des symptômes que des causes d’une crise qui s’est accumulée au fil des trente dernières années. L’érosion institutionnelle des forces armées les a rendues de plus en plus vulnérables à la subversion politique exercée par une présidence réactionnaire et imprévisible, qui a, au fond, accentué des faiblesses déjà profondément enracinées. Ces insuffisances se manifestent différemment dans chacune des branches de l’armée. Au sein de la marine, les dysfonctionnements organisationnels ont sapé les fondements matériels de la puissance maritime. Dans l’armée de l’air, la sophistication technologique coexiste avec une rigidité doctrinale quant aux capacités réelles de la puissance aérienne. Enfin, dans l’armée de terre et le Corps des Marines, la mise en avant d’une certaine conception du combattant – renforcée par le prestige acquis par les forces spéciales au cours de vingt années de lutte contre le terrorisme – a favorisé des formes de « prétorianisme » de plus en plus difficiles à concilier avec le professionnalisme militaire démocratique et les exigences pratiques d’une victoire décisive. Prises ensemble, ces trois crises posent une question qui a de profondes implications pour les alliés de Washington. Alors que les débats sur la fiabilité des États-Unis en tant que partenaire s’intensifient face au leadership erratique de Trump et à son obsession d’imposer des droits de douane, la question centrale concernant la position des États-Unis en tant que puissance mondiale ne se limite plus uniquement à la volonté de Washington d’exercer un leadership mondial. Il s'agit désormais de savoir si, après des décennies d'érosion institutionnelle, le pays continuera à disposer de la capacité militaire nécessaire pour le faire. L’échec organisationnel : le déclin matériel de la marine américaine Vu de l’extérieur, la marine américaine reste redoutable. Ses onze porte-avions, sa flotte de sous-marins nucléaires, ses forces opérationnelles interarmées avec le Corps des Marines ainsi que son réseau de bases lui confèrent une présence mondiale sans égale, lui permettant de relier l’océan Atlantique, l’océan Pacifique, la mer Méditerranée, l’océan Indien et le golfe Persique. La marine chinoise, qui connaît actuellement une expansion accélérée, ne dispose pas encore d’une infrastructure mondiale similaire. Ces capacités impressionnantes masquent toutefois l'état de plus en plus précaire de l'infrastructure maritime américaine. Pour un pays continental dont les intérêts économiques et stratégiques s’étendent à travers le monde, la puissance maritime est la condition préalable à presque toutes les autres capacités. Les avions, l’infanterie, les missiles et les forces d’opérations spéciales ne peuvent mener à bien des opérations militaires qu’avec des navires, des réseaux logistiques et des stocks prépositionnés. Cette réalité a souvent été occultée par l’admiration portée aux forces d’opérations spéciales et à leurs capacités d’attaque de pointe, la destruction spectaculaire d’une cible étant considérée comme l’essence même de la puissance militaire. Mais un avion F-35 ou un membre des forces spéciales dépendent en réalité d'un dispositif logistique colossal. Sans une infrastructure d’approvisionnement et de maintenance capable d’assurer le contrôle des voies maritimes mondiales et de garantir la capacité opérationnelle des navires de guerre, une grande partie de ce qui confère aux États-Unis leur supériorité militaire devient rapidement inutilisable. La crise structurelle qui menace ce système trouve son origine au début des années 1990 après l’effondrement de l’Union soviétique, lorsque la recherche du « dividende de la paix » a conduit à des coupes budgétaires qui ont réduit la flotte de la marine américaine de moitié en vingt ans. Parallèlement, après les attentats terroristes perpétrés par Al-Qaïda en septembre 2001, les principales ressources et l’attention politique ont été orientées vers les guerres terrestres et la lutte contre le terrorisme au Moyen-Orient. En raison de ces pressions financières supplémentaires, les fonctions de maintenance et d’approvisionnement, qui relevaient auparavant de la supervision gouvernementale, ont été externalisées, les capacités de construction navale ont été réduites et la flotte restante a dû maintenir une présence mondiale avec moins de navires et des équipages diminués. Confrontés à cette contradiction, les responsables de la marine ont cherché des solutions technologiques pour pallier les problèmes organisationnels. Le résultat le plus connu a été le programme Littoral Combat Ship How the Navy Spent Billions on Failed Littoral Combat Ship Program », ProPublica , 7 septembre 2023.'> 4 , qui, au lieu de fournir des navires modulaires et peu coûteux nécessitant de petits équipages, a cumulé défaillances techniques et dérives de coûts. « Il y a un écart croissant entre la puissance théorique et la puissance effective en mer. » Photo : AP/Sakchai Lalit « Les capacités impressionnantes de la marine américaine masquent l'état de plus en plus précaire de son infrastructure. » Photo : AP/Sakchai Lalit « Il y a un écart croissant entre la puissance théorique et la puissance effective en mer. » Photo : AP/Sakchai Lalit « Les capacités impressionnantes de la marine américaine masquent l'état de plus en plus précaire de son infrastructure. » Photo : AP/Sakchai Lalit Les problèmes liés à la modernisation de la flotte, notamment dans le cadre des programmes de porte-avions de classe Ford et de sous-marins de classe Columbia, ont été moins spectaculaires, mais révèlent des difficultés similaires et malgré des augmentations plus récentes des budgets consacrés à la construction navale, la marine n'est toujours pas parvenue à stabiliser la taille de sa flotte. Cela s'explique notamment par une pénurie de main-d’œuvre qualifiée et par des processus d’acquisition qui prennent régulièrement des risques technologiques avant que les conceptions ne soient au point, ce qui a entraîné des retards dans de nombreux programmes. La crise croissante de la maintenance, qui suscitait déjà des inquiétudes parmi les hauts responsables au début des années 2010, est encore plus préoccupante pour les responsables de la planification navale américaine. En août 2026, le Government Accountability Office a indiqué que les sous-marins nucléaires d’attaque avaient perdu plus de 15 000 jours opérationnels en raison de retards de maintenance et de temps d’immobilisation au cours de la décennie précédente. Dès lors, il y a un écart croissant entre la puissance théorique et la puissance effective en mer. Un navire immobilisé des mois en attente d’entretien reste inscrit au registre sans être déployable, et les crédits votés ne reconstituent pas au même rythme un vivier de soudeurs et d’ingénieurs ni un parc de cales sèches que des décennies de sous-investissement ont laissé se réduire. Ces dysfonctionnements organisationnels sont tels que la marine américaine peine à pallier les pénuries de pièces de rechange et de personnel de maintenance qualifié, même lorsque le Congrès alloue les fonds nécessaires. Depuis janvier 2025, la deuxième administration Trump a soumis ce système à des tensions supplémentaires. Le limogeage d’officiers expérimentés, comme l’ancienne cheffe des opérations navales, l’amiral Lisa Franchetti, et l’ancien chef du Commandement Sud, l’amiral Alvin Holsey, a été suivi d’une vague de départs plus large. De plus, des luttes de factions et l’incertitude politique ont entraîné une nouvelle perte de personnel au sein des institutions navales, et la guerre contre l’Iran a davantage exacerbé ces difficultés. Au cours des années 2010, la pression exercée sur les équipages en sous-effectif pour respecter de longs calendriers de déploiement contribuait déjà à l’épuisement du personnel et à une série d’accidents. Les déploiements de porte-avions, qui durent désormais la majeure partie de l’année, témoignent de la façon dont des engagements politiques dépassant la capacité organisationnelle à les honorer peuvent briser n’importe quelle institution d’État. L’échec doctrinal : la stagnation intellectuelle de l’armée de l’air américaine L'armée de l'air est confrontée à un problème plus difficile à cerner. Les États-Unis disposent toujours, et de loin, de la flotte la plus sophistiquée au monde en matière d'avions de combat, de capteurs, d'avions ravitailleurs, de bombardiers et de systèmes de soutien. Sa maîtrise de la frappe de cibles situées à des milliers de kilomètres avec des armes de précision reste unique. Cependant, au cœur de la crise que traverse l’armée de l’air se trouve une tendance persistante à confondre capacité de destruction et capacité à obtenir des victoires stratégiques durables. Depuis l’émergence de la théorie du bombardement stratégique, la force aérienne américaine s’est systématiquement appuyée sur l’idée que la supériorité technologique permettrait de contourner la réalité complexe et coûteuse de la guerre. Différentes générations ont formulé cette hypothèse de diverses manières, allant du bombardement stratégique et du blocus aérien aux frappes de précision, en passant par les opérations basées sur les effets et la stratégie de « shock and awe ». La priorité institutionnelle est toujours restée centrée sur les éléments vitaux dont dépend l’adversaire, dans le but de les détruire rapidement tout en limitant le recours à des opérations terrestres à grande échelle. L’expérience en Irak, en Afghanistan et, aujourd’hui, en Iran, illustre les limites d’une conception doctrinale qui avait déjà fait l’objet de critiques virulentes de la part de chercheurs tels que Robert Pape dans les années 1990. Certes, la puissance aérienne peut détruire les centres de commandement et le matériel, mais elle ne permet pas de déterminer de manière fiable comment le régime politique de l’ennemi réagira après la disparition de ces cibles. En effet, un adversaire peut se fragmenter plutôt que de se rendre, ou simplement subir des niveaux de destruction que les planificateurs américains jugent stratégiquement insensés. Il en résulte un écart flagrant entre l’excellence tactique et la déception stratégique qui caractérise la stratégie américaine. Comme les avions américains démontrent sans cesse leur capacité à dominer des adversaires conventionnels, l’échec peut toujours être imputé aux dirigeants politiques ou à une utilisation insuffisante de la force, et non aux principes fondamentaux de la doctrine elle-même. La supériorité technologique a également contribué à mettre l’accent sur des systèmes sophistiqués, dont le coût et la complexité rendent difficile leur déploiement rapide ou en quantité suffisante. Nous constatons déjà comment la prolifération des drones et des systèmes de missiles bon marché remet en cause un modèle dans lequel la maîtrise de l’espace aérien repose principalement sur un nombre restreint de plates-formes aux performances exceptionnelles, dont l’acquisition et la maintenance peuvent coûter des centaines de millions de dollars. Il faut également noter que certaines composantes de l’armée de l’air américaine reconnaissent désormais à quel point leur modèle risque de devenir obsolète. Le programme Doctrine 2035 Air Force Doctrine 2035 '> 5 identifie explicitement la nécessité d’éviter une « stagnation doctrinale », alors que l’intelligence artificielle, la miniaturisation et les difficultés logistiques transforment l’espace de combat. Les simulations de guerre pour 2026 ont précisément mis l’accent sur les vulnérabilités liées à la logistique et aux communications, que les anciennes conceptions de la suprématie technologique avaient tendance à reléguer au second plan. « Des engagements politiques dépassant la capacité organisationnelle à les honorer peuvent briser n'importe quelle institution d'État. » Photo : AP/Sakchai Lalit Le problème tient donc au fait que l’adaptation institutionnelle doit surmonter des décennies d’investissements, de structures de carrière et d’identités organisationnelles construites autour d’une conception bien établie de la suprématie aérienne. Malgré les efforts considérables de ses réformateurs, le chaos organisationnel et le limogeage arbitraire de dirigeants clefs sous l’administration Trump ont accru le risque que les nouvelles technologies soient intégrées à l'ancien cadre conceptuel plutôt que de forcer son évolution. L’échec stratégique en Iran est donc le symptôme de ce manque d’adaptation intellectuelle. Si la puissance aérienne américaine a détruit de nombreuses cibles, elle n’a pas réussi à obtenir rapidement des résultats décisifs face à des adversaires capables d’infliger des pertes aux réseaux logistiques et d’épuiser les stocks de missiles américains. Une doctrine militaire centrée sur la capacité de frapper n’importe où perd considérablement de son efficacité lorsque le problème est de pouvoir poursuivre la campagne alors que la millième frappe n'a toujours pas mis fin à la guerre. L’échec moral : la « prétorianisation » culturelle de l’armée de terre et du Corps des Marines des États-Unis La crise à laquelle sont confrontées les forces terrestres américaines est différente. L’armée de terre et le Corps des Marines conservent des capacités de combat redoutables et ont jusqu’à présent échappé à certaines des pressions matérielles auxquelles la marine est confrontée. Pourtant, derrière les questions d’approvisionnement et de préparation opérationnelle se cache une transformation potentiellement plus corrosive, qui a permis un glissement de l’idéal culturel à travers lequel certaines branches de l’armée américaine conçoivent la raison d'être d'un soldat. Ces changements fondamentaux dans la culture institutionnelle découlent de la manière dont vingt ans de « guerre contre le terrorisme » ont considérablement rehaussé le statut social des forces d’opérations spéciales. Les unités chargées de missions extrêmement spécialisées sont devenues un élément central de la force militaire. Plus important encore, dans la culture populaire et dans certaines franges de l’armée elle-même, elles sont considérées comme l’expression la plus pure de l’armée. Depuis 2001, le combattant d’élite a remplacé le « soldat-citoyen » comme idéal de l’identité militaire américaine. Il en résulte ce que l’on pourrait appeler un « culte des forces spéciales », sous la forme d’un récit semi-mythologique mettant en scène de petits groupes d’hommes dotés d’une puissance destructrice hors du commun, dont l’agressivité et les compétences leur permettent de surmonter les lourdes contraintes des institutions conventionnelles. Ces dynamiques ont été encore renforcées par les médias et les réseaux sociaux, qui présentent ces opérations spéciales de manière spectaculaire. Alors qu’un raid mené par une unité des SEAL offre des images impressionnantes à la télévision, le système d’approvisionnement qui garantit qu’un hélicoptère essentiel à l'accomplissement des missions recevra les pièces nécessaires à son fonctionnement n’a pas le même impact. Pourtant, l’efficacité militaire a toujours dépendu de ce système, bien plus que ne veulent l'admettre nos sociétés, fascinées par les images de soldats d’élite. L’effondrement de la stratégie militaire américaine en Afghanistan en 2021 a mis en évidence de manière flagrante des leçons stratégiques de longue date. Aucune quantité d’équipements sophistiqués ni aucune unité de commandos bien entraînée n’aurait pu protéger un pays dont les forces armées dépendaient de systèmes logistiques et de maintenance qu’elles ne pouvaient pas assurer elles-mêmes. La logique morale qui peut accompagner le culte du combattant est encore plus dangereuse. Si la létalité exceptionnelle devient la qualité militaire suprême, alors la retenue juridique, le contrôle civil et le respect des civils non combattants risquent d'être progressivement perçus comme des obstacles bureaucratiques imposés par des personnes qui ne comprennent rien à la guerre. Les militaires peuvent commencer alors à se percevoir comme des professionnels dotés de compétences uniques, appartenant à une caste morale supérieure, dont l’expérience de la violence leur confère une autorité décisive que les civils ne peuvent détenir. La polémique autour d’Eddie Gallagher Edward Gallagher : Navy Seals called platoon leader 'freaking evil' », BBC News , 28 décembre 2019.'> 6 , membre des Navy SEAL, au milieu des années 2010, illustre bien l’évolution de ces tendances culturelles. L’intervention publique de Hegseth en sa faveur, alors qu’il était encore commentateur chez Fox News en 2019, reflétait une dynamique politique plus large : les accusations de comportement inapproprié sur le champ de bataille pouvaient être perçues comme une preuve de l’authenticité du combattant, tandis que les juristes militaires et les commandants qui tentaient de faire respecter les normes professionnelles étaient présentés comme les ennemis de la létalité. Une fois ce raisonnement établi, la distinction entre une action militaire ciblée et une violence sauvage et aveugle a tendance à s'estomper. Hegseth a été profondément influencé par cette culture. L’accent qu’il met sur la restauration de l’« éthique guerrière » ( warrior ethos ), ses attaques contre les initiatives en faveur de la diversité et sa définition de la réforme militaire à travers un langage agressif et masculiniste axé sur la létalité confèrent une légitimité politique à des courants qui se sont développés depuis des décennies au sein des sous-cultures militaires américaines. « Une doctrine centrée sur la capacité de frapper n'importe où perd de son efficacité lorsque la millième frappe n'a toujours pas mis fin à la guerre. » Photo : AP/Sakchai Lalit « Trump et Hegseth sont autant des symptômes que des causes d'une crise qui s'est accumulée au fil des trente dernières années. » Photo : AP/Sakchai Lalit « Une doctrine centrée sur la capacité de frapper n'importe où perd de son efficacité lorsque la millième frappe n'a toujours pas mis fin à la guerre. » Photo : AP/Sakchai Lalit « Trump et Hegseth sont autant des symptômes que des causes d'une crise qui s'est accumulée au fil des trente dernières années. » Photo : AP/Sakchai Lalit Les implications dépassent le cadre des relations entre civils et militaires. Une armée qui glorifie les combattants risque en effet de mépriser les personnes sur lesquelles repose de plus en plus la guerre moderne : ingénieurs, logisticiens, analystes du renseignement, experts en drones, techniciens de maintenance, spécialistes en logiciels et officiers capables de tirer des enseignements des armées étrangères. L’anti-intellectualisme, souvent associé à une culture de combat axée sur la performance, a donc un impact sur le plan opérationnel, notamment parce qu’il encourage la croyance selon laquelle l’agressivité, la détermination et la volonté peuvent se substituer aux compétences institutionnelles. Pourtant, la guerre entre l’Ukraine et la Russie depuis 2022 enseigne la leçon inverse. La résilience ukrainienne repose en effet sur une capacité d'improvisation exceptionnelle pour mettre en place des réseaux d'approvisionnement, adapter les technologies de drones et intégrer des innovations sur le champ de bataille. Soixante ans plus tôt, les forces vietnamiennes avaient démontré de la même manière qu’aucun acte d’héroïsme sur le champ de bataille, aussi grand soit-il, ne pouvait résister à la puissance américaine sans le soutien de systèmes logistiques sophistiqués. Ce « prétorianisme » menace donc la puissance militaire américaine sur deux plans simultanément : sur le plan constitutionnel, il encourage les officiers et les soldats à se considérer comme les gardiens d’une certaine conception de la nation plutôt que comme les serviteurs des autorités civiles légitimement élues dans le cadre de l’ordre constitutionnel ; sur le plan opérationnel, il privilégie une conception de la virilité militaire de plus en plus dépassée, précisément à une époque où la guerre exige davantage de sophistication institutionnelle et de curiosité intellectuelle. Les dilemmes de l’Europe face au déclin des États-Unis Les États-Unis ne cesseront pas d’être une grande puissance du jour au lendemain. Le pays dispose de ressources économiques considérables, d’une infrastructure militaire sans égale, de réserves exceptionnelles d’expertise technologique, et aucun des processus décrits n’est irréversible. Les leçons à en tirer pour les Européens et les autres alliés se situent ailleurs : pour inverser cette tendance et éviter le dysfonctionnement stratégique des États-Unis, il faut reconnaître la nature systémique du déclin militaire américain. Les ressources financières ne suffiront pas à elles seules à redonner vie à des chantiers navals dont la main-d’œuvre qualifiée a disparu. De même, des avions plus performants ne peuvent pas pallier une doctrine qui confond destruction et succès stratégique. De plus, la réflexion de Pete Hegseth sur l’« éthique guerrière » ne peut compenser l’érosion des normes professionnelles, des compétences logistiques et de l’ouverture d’esprit. L’Europe est désormais confrontée à trois dilemmes qui se recoupent. À court terme, elle doit combler le fossé entre la crédibilité américaine et le temps nécessaire à son réarmement, et ce, non seulement face à la Russie, mais aussi dans la région atlantique et en Méditerranée. À moyen terme, les Européens doivent déterminer quels éléments du système de défense américain sont réellement essentiels, lesquels imposeraient une charge financière intenable, et dans quels domaines des partenariats avec le Canada, le Japon et d'autres grandes puissances démocratiques pourraient garantir la résilience mondiale. À plus long terme, ils pourraient être contraints de renégocier les bases d'une relation transatlantique dans une dynamique complètement différente, avec des capacités militaires accrues d'un côté, et des États-Unis affaiblis, mais toujours puissants de l'autre. Depuis 1945, les Européens ont relevé d'importants défis en matière de sécurité, avec le soutien militaire des États-Unis. La confiance dans cette relation, profondément ancrée, apparaît désormais comme dangereuse et complaisante. La question stratégique à laquelle l’Union européenne et le Royaume-Uni sont confrontés est donc l'inverse de la boutade d'Henry Kissinger qui disait que Washington ne savait pas qui appeler lorsqu’il voulait joindre l’Europe. Des décennies plus tard, les Européens sont désormais confrontés à la possibilité que, lorsqu'ils feront appel aux États-Unis, il n'y ait peut-être plus d'Amérique capable de répondre à leur appel. L’article L’armée américaine ne sait plus faire la guerre est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .

items.title: El acta de nacimiento del ‘R3’, el nuevo jefe del Cartel Jalisco, revela datos inéditos sobre sus orígenes en California
items.description: En los espacios destinados para poner la información del padre aparece la abreviatura “N/A” por “No aplica”. Así quedó oculto el nombre de Armando Valencia Cornelio, uno de los fundadores del Cartel del Milenio. El recién nacido registrado en esa acta de nacimiento, emitida por el Gobierno de California, era Juan Carlos Valencia González también conocido como R3 . Cuatro décadas después se convertiría en el primer jefe de una organización mexicana de tráfico de drogas —el Cartel Jalisco Nueva Generación (CJNG)— que nació en territorio estadounidense, una enorme paradoja ante la retórica antidrogas del Gobierno de Donald Trump. Seguir leyendo

items.title: GH¢299m COVID fumigation spending audited but left out of report, says Manasseh Awuni
items.description: Investigative journalist Manasseh Azure Awuni says the Audit Service has confirmed it audited GH¢299 million spent by the Ministry of Local Government on COVID-19 fumigation, even though the expenditure was omitted from its final report. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Tuesday, he said he wrote to the Audit Service to establish why the Ministry’s fumigation expenditure was missing from the Auditor-General’s report on COVID-19 spending. He said the Audit Service provided him with an appendix listing the ministries covered by the audit, including the Ministry of Local Government. “But beyond that, I specifically mentioned the Ministry of Local Government and also fumigation, and the Audit Service indeed told me that they audited everything, all the expenditure, whatever money they took and spent, they audited everything, including the fumigation.” According to Mr Awuni, the Audit Service’s response was that the omission of the expenditure from the report did not mean the spending had not been audited. “And their response to that question was that the fact that they did not include it didn’t mean that it was not audited.” The admission has raised questions about why the expenditure was not reflected in the COVID-19 audit report, particularly because the Ministry of Local Government spent GH¢299 million on fumigation. Mr Awuni said the Auditor-General’s report had put the total cost of fumigation at GH¢96 million. “So if you audited this ministry, which spent 299 million Ghana cedis on fumigation, they gave you the figures, you say you audited, why didn’t you capture it?” He said the omission was significant because one of the stated objectives of the audit was to provide a fair representation of COVID-19 revenues and expenditure. “When you look at the audit objectives, one of them, and they actually repeated that in my letter, was to give a fair representation of what was taken and what was spent.” Mr Awuni said the audit was therefore not solely about identifying wrongdoing. “It wasn’t so much about only wrongdoing. They also wanted, Okay, we took this much as a nation for COVID-19, and this is how much we spent.” He said the Audit Service’s explanation did not adequately address the omission of the Local Government Ministry’s spending. “So if you have huge figures spent by whole ministries totally omitted, I don’t think this response was so satisfactory.” Mr Awuni’s latest investigation into COVID-19 expenditure has focused on discrepancies between spending identified in government records and the figures in the Auditor-General’s COVID-19 audit report. The Audit Service’s confirmation that the Local Government Ministry’s fumigation expenditure was audited but not included in the final report now forms a key part of the investigation.

Why petrol remains expensive despite local refining— Dangote
items.description: *Notes having a male heir not his priority *Says ‘I’ve lived in my current home for 36 years’ By Juliet Umeh THE President of Dangote Group, Aliko Dangote, has said Nigerians were still paying high prices for petrol despite the commencement of large-scale domestic refining, saying local production does not completely insulate the country from global crude oil prices and market disruptions. Dangote, who spoke in an interview on Arise TV yesterday, said the refinery bought crude at prevailing market prices and sometimes paid significant premiums, making it impossible to sell petroleum products below sustainable market levels. Responding to concerns over high petrol prices, he said expensive was relative, arguing that fuel prices in neighbouring countries remained significantly higher than in Nigeria. According to him, “there is still a lot of smuggling of the same petrol we are producing to our neighbouring countries because those neighbouring countries are about 30 per cent to 50 per cent more expensive than Nigeria.” Dangote said the refinery had purchased crude for as much as $124 per barrel in May, adding that “we can’t go now and subsidise everything.” He, however, assured: “Nigerians don’t need to worry. There will not be any shortage from our own part. There will be no queues, and we’ll make sure we keep satisfying the market despite all odds.” On Nigeria’s industrialisation challenge, Dangote identified high borrowing costs as a major obstacle to new investments. “It is very difficult to industrialise with interest rates at 30 percent. I can’t see the magician who can actually industrialise a country with 30 per cent interest cost,” he said. He warned that without policies deliberately protecting domestic investments, Nigeria might struggle to attract another major refinery project. He warned: “Under the current things that are going on, especially downstream, I cannot see any new refinery in our lifetime. “Government must protect productive domestic industries if it expects businesses to create jobs, generate taxes and deepen economic activities. “If you import, what you are doing is you are importing poverty and exporting jobs that you are supposed to create out of the country,” he said. Dangote also identified inconsistent government policies and inadequate electricity as persistent obstacles to manufacturing, declaring “you cannot manufacture goods with diesel.” ‘I’ve lived in my current home for 36 years’ Speaking further, Dangote revealed he had lived in his current home for 36 years, saying he had no plans to move because he was comfortable there. “You know how long I’ve been here? Thirty-six years. I don’t plan on leaving. I’m very comfortable here,” he said. The billionaire, who not ed that he was generally content with his home and didn’t feel the need to constantly seek out new luxuries, said: “Once I come in in the evening, it’s difficult to take me out of my house.” Dangote also spoke about the spending habits of some wealthy Africans, criticising those who acquired private jets without investing in productive ventures such as factories. “What I see is people now owning aircraft all over the place, flying all over, and they don’t have one single factory. “So it means that they’re not actually helping in growing the economy, and that has to change,” he said. He said his priority was to use his wealth and business interests to contribute to the industrialisation of Africa, stressing that his biggest legacy would be to help build productive capacity on the continent. Dangote also said foreign investors were increasingly interested in Africa but needed large-scale investment opportunities capable of attracting substantial capital. “Foreigners are very interested now; they want to invest in Africa, but they don’t have big-ticket items. “So right now, they have started seeing big-ticket stuff, and they will join. And we will join to develop our own continent, Africa,” he added. Having a male heir not my priority On succession, Dangote said not having a son to inherit his business empire was not a priority, stressing that his three daughters were capable of taking over the Dangote Group. He stated this on Tuesday, where he said he believed one of his daughters could eventually lead the conglomerate. Asked whether he could see one of his daughters taking charge of the group, Dangote said: “I think, yes, I can see one of them. I’ve been watching all of them, so I can definitely see one of the three that can actually lead. Recall that Dangote’s daughters, Halima, Fatima and Mariya, hold senior positions within the conglomerate, with their roles expanding as the group continues to develop its succession structure. Dangote said their involvement in the family business was based on their personal interest rather than pressure from him. “They are very, very interested in the business. I’m not forcing them to come and be part of this business, no. They are very interested, and they enjoy it,” he said. The billionaire and Africa’s richest man said he believed his daughters could surpass his achievements and take the company to a higher level. “One of them can be better than — I never expected to perform this much. But I’m sure they’re highly educated, so they will be more creative. So most likely, they might be even taking the company to the next level,” he said. Asked if he believed all three daughters were capable of achieving this, Dangote replied: “All of them.” On whether he still hoped to have a son, particularly given the traditional expectations surrounding male heirs in Kano, Dangote said it was not important to him. “Sometimes you can pray for God to give you a son, but that son might be the one to bring down the name of the family. “Sometimes when God doesn’t give you something, don’t push. I don’t think a son would have done something better than these three daughters that I have. That one, I think, you know, it’s not my priority,” he said. Dangote added that having a male heir did not necessarily guarantee the preservation of a family legacy. “God controls everything. And for me, really, sometimes, yeah, you can pray for God to give you a son, but that son might be the one that would tear down the name of the family,” he said. However, Dangote said his broader succession plan was not simply about transferring control of the conglomerate to a family member, but ensuring that the company was professionally managed. “I want this company to be run professionally. I want to have the highest level of governance,” he said. He cited global companies such as Microsoft and Apple as examples of businesses that had continued to thrive beyond their founders. “We want to make sure that we make it very difficult for any family member to come and destroy anything. The businessman said his ultimate legacy was to contribute to the industrialisation of Africa. “What I want to leave as a legacy is to industrialise Africa. I cannot do it alone, but I’m 100% sure that in the next two or three years, other Africans will join,” he said. items.title: Need for speedy reconstruction of police barracks
items.description: Inspector-General of Police Olatunji Disu’s recent inspection of police barracks under reconstruction in Lagos has exposed a painful reality: decades of neglect have turned many police quarters into slums unfit for human habitation. His frustration over delays in completing the projects is understandable. But beyond expressing frustration, the inspection must translate into urgency, accountability and tangible results. The scale of the Lagos intervention is significant, though still inadequate in relation to the national crisis. Disu inspected about 21 barracks and housing projects, with at least 1,000 housing units expected to be delivered by February 2027 through collaboration involving the Lagos State Government and private developers. This is commendable, but the problem extends far beyond Lagos. The Federal Government’s rehabilitation of 13 police training colleges nationwide also acknowledges the deplorable condition of facilities that have undermined police training for decades. Across Nigeria, reports of dilapidated barracks paint a disturbing picture. Officers and their families live in overcrowded rooms, share inadequate sanitary facilities and endure unreliable water supplies, damaged buildings and generally unhealthy surroundings. It is difficult to demand the highest standards of discipline and public order from officers whose own living environments are overwhelmed by neglect and squalor. More troubling is that only a fraction of police personnel reside in barracks. Most officers live in rented accommodation among civilians, often at considerable cost and sometimes in environments that expose them and their families to security risks. This arrangement can also undermine rapid mobilisation, particularly when officers have to travel considerable distances to their duty posts during emergencies. Decent accommodation should therefore not be treated merely as a welfare benefit. It is an element of policing infrastructure. Officers who live in secure, hygienic and properly maintained quarters are likely to enjoy better morale and a stronger sense of belonging. Proper accommodation can also facilitate unit cohesion and rapid response. Conversely, poor housing imposes financial, psychological and operational burdens that can diminish efficiency and discipline. The Federal Government and the police authorities must consequently make police housing a national security priority. The Lagos approach, involving government support, private-sector participation and mortgage financing, deserves to be expanded to other states. Corporate organisations, wealthy individuals and development institutions that often enjoy exclusive police protection should also be encouraged to support the reconstruction or adoption of specific barracks. However, such partnerships must be transparent to prevent situations of police sell-out to powerful individuals and organisations. The dignity of the Nigeria Police Force cannot be restored while officers and their families live in decrepitude. Disu’s inspection should therefore be the beginning of a sustained nationwide housing programme, not just a ceremonial tour. A police force expected to protect citizens must itself be treated with dignity. The time for excuses is over. Let’s act fast! items.title: Naira appreciates to N1,380/$ in parallel market
items.description: By Elizabeth Adegbesan The Naira yesterday appreciated to N1,380 per dollar from N1,390 in the parallel market on Monday. But the naira depreciated to N1,329.5 per dollar in the Nigerian Foreign Exchange Market, NFEM. Data from the Central Bank of Nigeria, CBN, showed that the indicative exchange rate for the naira rose to N1,329.5 per dollar from N1,329 per dollar on Monday, indicating 50 kobo depreciation for the local currency. Consequently, the margin between the parallel and official markets narrowed to N50.5 per dollar from N61 per dollar on Monday. The value of interbank turnover in NFEM grew by 177.6 percent to $262.12 million from $94.4 million on Monday. items.title: Karachi: how much dirtier?
items.description: AS they say everything comes at a cost — and so does Karachi’s ranking as one of the least liveable cities. Karachi has slipped from the seventh least liveable city in 2021 to the fourth least liveable one in 2026. It ranks 170th among the 173 cities surveyed by the Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU). This decline has come despite enormous spending by the Sindh government — estimated at around Rs126 billion in these five years alone — to garbage-collection contractors. Since 2017, including the current year’s allocation, spending on garbage collection and street sweeping is estimated to exceed Rs190bn, with an estimated Rs160-170bn spent in the name of Karachi alone. No other initiative has received such generous provincial financing over the past decade — not the BRT Red Line, the BRT Yellow Line, the K-IV water supply project, the Safe City project, Karachi’s road network, not even the Right Bank Outfall Drain, which is critical to rural Sindh’s economy. When the EIU measures liveability, environmental quality is only one of five major criteria, with cleanliness forming a sub-component. However, on Numbeo’s global pollution index, Karachi continues to rank as one of the world’s most polluted cities with a pollution index score of 89.5/100. This index evaluates air quality, drinking water availability, garbage disposal, cleanliness, water pollution, noise and light pollution, green spaces, and overall comfort. Across all these metrics, garbage disposal has remained the poorest performer despite billions being spent by the Sindh Solid Waste Management Board (SSWMB) under the chief minister’s chairmanship. In 2016, the Sindh government took over the mu­­nicipal functions of garbage collection and stre­­et sweeping — previously managed by the KMC and union councils — and outsourced them to foreign firms. The contracts covered door-to-door collection, sweeping of streets, lanes, medians, footpaths and open spaces, transportation to transfer stations and landfills, provision of bins and compactors, deployment of sanitary workers, and GPS-based monitoring. Initially introduced across Karachi’s districts, the outsourcing model was later extended to Hyderabad, Sukkur and Larkana. The city’s dismal ranking on the liveability and pollution indexes reflects a crisis of governance more than a shortage of funds. The system was designed around a simple principle: garbage should not remain on the ground. Mini-trucks were to collect waste door to door and from designated bins, feed it into compactors at district collection centres, and ensure its transportation to landfill sites the same day. Uncollected areas, roadside garbage, failure to deploy prescri­bed staff or machinery, and other performance lap­­­­ses attracted financial penalties. Vehicles were to be GPS-tracked, while manual sweeping supplemented mechanical cleaning. A command-and-control system linked to the SSWMB headquarters was to monitor fleet movements; an independent firm was to verify the contractors’ performan­ce; and complaints were to be resolved within eight hours. Going by these performance indicators — and an estimated public-sector price tag approaching Rs170bn for the city over the period — Karachi should have become one of the cleanest cities in the region during the past decade. Yet the reality across much of the city is different. Open plots continue to serve as informal garbage dumps. Door-to-door collection remains patchy or is altogether absent in many localities. Waste continues to accumulate along the roads, open spaces and drains. Elected representatives themselves frequently complain about inadequate responsiveness by solid-waste contractors. Karachi continues to be ranked as one of the dirtiest cities all these 10 years. A review of these contracts against the ground realities over the past decade suggests that strict enforcement of the built-in penalty clauses should have driven non-compliant contractors into bankruptcy. The obvious question is: how have contractors been able to operate with such visible gaps between contractual obligations and conditions on the ground? The answer lies in two major contract and statutory violations by the provincial administration itself. First, the Sindh government has failed to hire an independent consulting firm for third-party verification since 2017, effectively granting contractors a decade-long exemption from performance audits. Second, the government has bypassed Section 14(3) of the Sindh Solid Waste Management Act, 2021, which states: “The executive directors of the board shall be appointed by the chief minister either from cadre service officers working under the control of government having relevant professional qualification and experience or from private sector through a competitive process possessing the requisite qualifications and experience of the post.” Despite managing contracts valued at Rs30-40bn, a key oversight position, such as director mo­­nito­ring and evaluation, has been filled by an of­­f­icer from the Benazir Income Support Prog­ram­­me. Compounding the issue is the lack of parliame­nt­a­­ry oversight. Reports from the Auditor General of Pakistan from 2018 through 2025 have repeatedly highlighted losses of billions of rupees by the SSWMB due to payments made without third-par­­ty verification, uncollected penalties, in­­ade­quate staffing, and overpayments. Yet, no effective corrective action has been taken all these years. The State of Governance in Pakistan, 2023, based on a nationwide household survey by TDEA/ Fafen, found 65 per cent of Karachi respondents to be dissatisfied with garbage disposal services, while another 22pc had no service available in their locality. So, 87pc of Karachi households surveyed were either dissatisfied with garbage disposal or had no service — a remarkable outcome after years of outsourcing and billions of rupees spent on solid-waste management. After chairing the board for seven years, starting in 2014, the chief minister transferred the steering committee to the local government minister in 2021, and operational supervision was handed to the mayor of Karachi in 2024. However, meaningful coordination with elected town chairmen and union councils to hold contractors accountable remains absent. In fact, despite their poor performance, SSWMB contractors were rewarded with a 42pc increase in payment, raising their annual bill from Rs28.3bn in 2024-25 to Rs40.3bn in 2025-26. Like many of Karachi’s challenges, the real bottleneck has not been the shortage of funds for the Sindh government, but poor governance and lack of accountability. With the country’s economic engine ranking among the lowest on the liveability index and among the highest on the pollution index, all our aspirations for the country’s progress will remain a pipe dream. The writer is former federal secretary, caretaker provincial minister and currently chairman, Policy Research and Advisory Council. Published in Dawn, September 16th, 2026

items.title: Dangerous escalation
items.description: JUST weeks after its formation, the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement faces its first challenge: the escalating conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthi militia . The rebel group has struck Saudi air bases and key oil facilities with missiles and drones, while the kingdom has intensified air strikes on Houthi-held areas in Yemen. The Houthis have also targeted Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea. The escalation began in mid-July, when the Houthis formally declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia and began hitting Saudi-flagged shipping, after Yemeni government forces attacked a flight from Iran at Sana’a airport. The Houthis have been fighting Yemen’s internationally recognised government since 2014. The violence subsided after the warring sides reached an internationally brokered ceasefire in 2022, but flared up again after the July incident when the militia broke the truce, declared a blockade on Saudi shipping in the Red Sea and began attacking Saudi vessels. Its ultimate aim is to drive Saudi Arabia out of Yemen and take full control of the territory. This latest escalation has widened the conflict in West Asia, even as America’s war with Iran grinds on with no end in sight. With the fighting now threatening Saudi Arabia directly, will the kingdom invoke the alliance’s mutual defence clause — the one that treats an attack on one member as an attack on all members? The danger of a wider conflagration engulfing the entire region carries serious implications for the rest of the world. The Houthis, who already hold much of Yemen, have seized a strategic island in a lightning offensive against government forces, giving them complete control of Bab al-Mandeb — the key marine chokepoint through which 12 per cent of the world’s trade passes. They now control 90 per cent of Yemen’s Red Sea coastline. The Houthi leadership says it is not seeking to block all commercial shipping in the Red Sea, only Saudi-linked vessels. But the heightening tension is likely to keep other ships away. With the Strait of Hormuz virtually blocked, the situation is explosive. Global energy markets, already reeling from the six-month conflict between US-Israel and Iran, are bracing for further shock. Saudi Arabia, which had stayed out of the Iran war, now risks being drawn into a wider conflict. These actions by a militia widely seen as aligned with Iran have opened a new front in the conflict. They have coincided with a drone attack, apparently launched from Iraq by allegedly another Iran-linked militia, that forced temporary closure of the East-West oil pipeline crossing Saudi Arabia. Together, the attacks have disrupted Saudi oil exports. It is widely accepted that Iran backs the Houthis, though the group also operates independently of Tehran. The attacks on Saudi Arabia are certainly not in Iran’s interest while it is engaged in an existential war with the US — the fallout is already visible. Saudi Arabia, which had so far kept itself out of the Iran war, is now in danger of being drawn into a wider regional conflict. Although Iran has distanced itself from the attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure by the two militias, the incidents have heightened tensions between Riyadh and Tehran. Following the attacks, talks between Iran and the Gulf states aimed at reopening the Strait of Hormuz were postponed . It would have been the first meeting between Iran and the main GCC member states in two years; the meeting, to be held in Oman, was part of an effort to find a regional solution allowing free passage through the critical waterway. The latest flare-up has thwarted that effort. As the fighting spreads, Saudi Arabia finds itself on the front line. In the latest turn, the kingdom reportedly sought American military help , only to be turned down by President Donald Trump, who said the Houthis had assured him they did not want to expand the conflict. The development has given an intriguing twist to the conflict. Trump’s response is said to be driven by his frustration with the kingdom for failing to actively support his war against Iran. America and Israel have carried out missile strikes against the Houthis in the past over their support for the Palestinian resistance. But there is also the question of whether US intervention in the Saudi-Houthi conflict will help stabilise a situation for which Washington is itself responsible. The growing tension between Iran and Saudi Ara­bia will only serve the US agenda in the region. So far, Saudi Arabia has not formally invoked the Makkah defence alliance clause, which would require Pakistan and Turkiye to come to its def­ence if it is attacked. But consultations are under way as the conflict spreads. Diplomatic efforts to halt the Houthis’ escalatory moves are still continuing. Reportedly, Pakistan’s military chief and the Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan both spoke to Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi. Pakistan is also believed to have conveyed a Saudi message urging Iran to rein in the Houthis, and reminded Tehran of Islamabad’s own pact commitment to Riyadh. Defence Minister Khawaja Asif recently said that unprovoked aggression against the kingdom, or a spillover into it, would make the pact operational — “there should be no doubt about that”. Earlier, in April 2026, Saudi Arabia’s defence ministry announced that a Pakistani military contingent had arrived at King Abdulaziz Air Base, with fighter and support aircraft, under a bilateral defence pact signed in September 2025 . Following Khawaja Asif’s remarks, however, the Foreign Office spokesperson said , “I don’t think we should be discussing this topic in the context of its operationalisation”. The situation remains dangerous for both Pakistan and the larger region, and the widening conflict could suck in even those countries that have kept out of the Iran war and have been trying to help broker a negotiated end to it. Pakistan needs to tread a more cautious path in a conflict that could prove disastrous for the country. It’s a perilous escalation that needs to be resolved through negotiations rather than war. The writer is an author and journalist. zhussain100@yahoo.com X: @hidhussain Published in Dawn, September 16th, 2026

items.title: What is Peter Obi looking for in Yelwata? By Rotimi Fasan
items.description: Now that he has been given a fresh invite by so-called elders of the community to visit after last week’s botched attempt, I think it is legitimate to ask what Peter Obi, the National Democratic Congress’s presidential candidate, is looking for in Yelwata, a somnolent town in Benue State, at a time when he should be campaigning for the mandate of Nigerians in the January 16, 2027 presidential election? The lacklustre nature of the campaigns was the subject of this column last week. Then I wrote about the apparent indifference of the presidential candidates to the election campaigns, unlike the case in the 2023 election. If President Bola Tinubu, the candidate of the ruling All Progressives Congress—a party with a vast network of structures and which could count on the support of 31 state governors across party lines—if that party’s candidate could choose to take three weeks off on what his minders have called a working vacation to Europe, does that give candidates of the other parties the licence to waste their time on idle activities, knowing how much they still have to do to begin to be seen as measuring up to the ruling party? These are leaders of political parties that are too quick to accuse the ruling party and, indeed, the president of constricting the democratic space. Even though there are nearly two dozen political parties registered for the 2027 election, leading opposition parties’ leaders have constantly accused the president of distracting them with hostile actors planted in these parties to foment trouble while pushing the country into a one-party state. But now that they have the opportunity to push their agenda through well-coordinated campaigns, they have left substance to chase shadows. Each week, a new outrage is manufactured. Last week it was the news of Peter Obi being barred from visiting Yelwata. That was framed as an attack, which Obi and his followers promoted, even when there was no assault of any kind. This week, it is the distraction of his wife’s multimillion-naira Hermes, a N245 million blot on the conscience of a moral crusader’s wife. That amount of money could well take the IDPs Obi purported to visit out of the camps and have them resettled in their homes. But this master of subterfuge and self-claimed possessor of one wristwatch and one black shoe would not see this. What, for goodness’ sake, could Peter Obi be doing on the road to Yelwata when he has the onerous task of making his case for the presidency to Nigerians? Why would he engage in the distraction of visiting an IDP camp at a time when he had the opportunity to put his waning electoral strength and relevance on an even keel? Is it because Peter Obi is so politically naïve that he does not recognise the enormity of the task ahead of him? Of course not. Obi knows exactly what he is doing. He is not so obtuse at the game as not to know he should be neck- and head-deep in the campaigns. He has no agenda for Nigeria. Would a man with a plan for the country be seen at the campaign event of a rival, selling the candidacy of that rival, as he did for Seyi Makinde, the presidential candidate of the Allied Peoples Party, during the inauguration of their campaign office? Which serious politician does that? Is this what they do in Bangladesh? Did he see Prime Minister Tarique Rahman of the Bangladesh National Party campaign for the candidate of the opposition Bangladesh Awami League? No! But as Datti Baba-Ahmed, his running mate in the 2023 election, has said to clarify why he had to leave Obi (Obi did not drop him as his running mate, he said) to his shenanigans while he sought his electoral fortune elsewhere, Peter Obi has no plan for Nigeria. That is not a new insight, however shocking it may sound coming from the former running mate of the man in question. It is something anyone who understands Peter Obi’s kind of politics, or what he represents as a politician, knows too well. The man simply has no plan for Nigeria beyond the weight of his campaign rhetoric. He is the product and hostage of a separatist formation with fascist tendencies that comes straight out of a hate-filled strain of Igbo nationalism. He is, at best, a political drifter who suddenly found himself at the centre of national attention he neither worked for nor prepared for, due to a convergence of freak occurrences during the 2023 election cycle. He lacks the political awareness to see himself as a historic figure who has been providentially placed to be in the vanguard of an incipient demographic that could change the political direction of the country. This, even if he did not prepare for it. But he frittered away the opportunity and took solace in divisive politics. The Peter Obi 2027 campaign lacks the unanticipated gravitas of its 2023 predecessor. It is a flotilla caught in an ocean of icebergs and is headed for nowhere. Outside its south-east enclave, it has no prospects, and Peter Obi, the supposed helmsman, knows this. Which is why he would abandon the campaign trail and make a beeline to an IDP camp in far-flung Yelwata. The man knows the game he is playing. Going to an IDP camp at this moment is part of his sleight of hand—a major aspect of his divisive politics through which his supporters push his narrative of Igbo victimisation. He is a demagogue who knows how to trigger his opponents, as his trip to Yelwata was bound to do. For want of a better strategy, Obi turns everything into politics. The horrible massacre in Yelwata occurred in June 2025, and Obi waited for more than a year for the campaigns to begin before choosing to go there on a campaign mission (where he doles out a few millions, typically about N10 million, where others give far more), which he disguises as a humanitarian visit. At the end of the visit, he drops a few broadsides against the government for failure to provide security and ensure the welfare of the people, while blaming the ruling party for the condition in which the people have found themselves; rounding up with his signature line—‘A New Nigeria is Possible’. Doing any of this at this time is not even a subtle attempt at campaigning. It is riling the people up for electoral revolt. Peter Obi is a coward of a politician who, rather than confront his opponents on the field, would go behind them to stir revolt in their backyard. He should drop his worn strategy of self-victimisation and milking of both the real and often fabricated grievances of his people. If you’d like, I can also produce a version that tightens syntax and improves flow without changing your argument or voice. The post What is Peter Obi looking for in Yelwata? By Rotimi Fasan appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Telecel CEO Obo-Nai champions integrity in leadership
items.description: Chief Executive Officer of Telecel Ghana, Patricia Obo-Nai, has made a case for leadership that combines excellence and competence with integrity, courage and a strong sense of responsibility to society. Speaking at the Commencement Ceremony of Palm University College in Manya Jorpanya, Shai Hills, Ms Obo-Nai reiterated the role of educational institutions in training ethical leaders. She said, “Through education, we can shape individuals into moral citizens who are capable of making informed decisions about their actions and their impact on society. “Ethics must, therefore, be intentionally integrated into the curriculum, reinforced through example, and practised through everyday decision-making” “Our country is calling for ethical leaders. Investors are looking for hands they can trust with their hard-earned money. “Employers are looking not only for people who can do the job, but for people whose judgement, discipline and character strengthen the organisations they join. “Technical expertise may open the door, but integrity is what sustains trust, builds brands and creates lasting value.” She added. The ceremony, held on the theme “The Quest to Educate Ethical and Excellent Leaders in Ghana,” brought together members of the Board of Trustees, faculty, students, parents, traditional leaders, industry partners, and friends of the University. In his address, the Founder and President of Palm University College, Dr Peter Carlos Okantey, said Palm University was founded on a simple but urgent conviction — that Ghana’s development challenges are not just a lack of skills, but a lack of ethical leadership. “Our university is built on the foundations of intellectual rigour, innovation and a commitment to ethical leadership in action. We have always placed a high premium on integrity, leadership and excellence. “I therefore implore all graduates to exhibit and apply the values, skills and talents that have been nurtured in you over the past several years. These values – integrity, leadership and excellence, if applied diligently, can help you navigate all the challenges and opportunities you will encounter,” Dr Okantey said. He further noted that through initiatives such as the Centre for Ethical Leadership (CEL), the Palm Corporate Mentoring Program, and the Palm GreenLab Innovation and Incubation Lab, the University is bridging the gap between classroom theory and real-world impact. In support of these initiatives, Ing. Obo-Nai announced the “Telecel Award for Excellence and Ethical Leadership” to promote ethics and excellence. Sponsored by Telecel Ghana, the annual award will be presented to a graduating student who has performed strongly academically and demonstrated sound judgement, integrity, responsibility, and service during their time at Palm University. Reflecting on his academic journey, one of the two valedictorians of the day, Dr Alex Osei, who graduated with an MSc in Services Management and Leadership, noted that the intrinsic desire for excellence, humility, and the impact of choices as a leader are what attracted him to the programme. He said, “Ethical leadership, as we have learnt in this programme, means making the harder right choice when no one is watching. It means transparency when it might be more convenient, and perhaps profitable, to conceal. It means equity and accountability when it is easier to deflect and blame.”

items.title: 2027: APC govs at daggers-drawn with Wike
items.description: ***Why we moved against Wike’s Rainbow Coalition – APC govs ***Warn against parallel structures By Omeiza Ajayi ABUJA – State governors elected on the platform of All Progressives Congress, APC, were at daggers drawn with Federal Capital Territory, FCT, Abuja Minister, Mr. Nyesom Wike, yesterday, over creation of parallel political structures believed capable of undermining President Bola Tinubu’s re-election bid in 2027. In a position widely seen as a direct response to the Rainbow Coalition championed by Wike, Chairman of the Progressive Governors Forum and Imo State governor, Senator Hope Uzodimma, who Wike had recently accused of sponsoring political attacks against him, made the declaration on behalf of the governors late Monday night, after a closed-door meeting at the Imo State Governor’s Lodge in Abuja. The warning comes amid mounting friction within the APC over the coalition, with some powerful blocs in the party said to be pushing back against the arrangement over fears that it could split votes and damage Tinubu’s 2027 presidential chances. The governors warned that coalition candidates flying different party flags could confuse rural voters, with the tensions already playing out in states, including Rivers, Kwara, Gombe and Cross River. Uzodimma stated that no arrangement that creates confusion, divided loyalty or competing interests within the party will be entertained. According to him, the primary focus of the forum is to support official APC candidates at all levels, rather than external interests. “The APC Governors Forum unanimously resolved that its members will not participate in, support or endorse any alliance or political arrangement capable of undermining the re-election of Mr President, weakening the APC or adversely affecting any candidate of the party at all levels. “In other words, the forum has no intention to support any candidate at any level that is not an APC candidate because our candidates who are contesting the election are being sponsored by our party. “The governors’ campaign commitment is exclusive to APC candidates. All levels of the party campaign architecture will align with the expectations of Mr President and the strategic objectives of the party,” Uzodimma said. The Progressives governors also pledged to take charge of President Tinubu’s re-election campaign across their respective states. Uzodimma, who read the communique, said the governors will not participate in any political alliance or arrangement capable of undermining President Tinubu’s re-election bid or weakening the APC. The warning against parallel structures has been read in some quarters as an indirect message to Wike, who remains a registered member of the Peoples Democratic Party, PDP, but has continued to insist that the Rainbow Coalition exists solely to secure Tinubu’s re-election. A political storm has been gathering across the length and breadth of Nigeria since Wike’s Rainbow Coalition swept through some states, upturning old loyalties, splitting ruling party ranks, and leaving governors, senators and grassroots politicians scrambling to recalibrate their positions ahead of the 2027 general election. From the ancient city of Ilorin to the creeks of Rivers State, from the hills of Cross River to the plains of Gombe, the coalition’s tentacles are reshaping the political map in ways that have left even seasoned watchers of Nigerian politics struggling to keep pace. Wike fights back, slams Uzodimma In a quick counter, the FCT minister queried why Uzodinma was unable to garner massive support for President Tinubu in the 2023 election, saying modern politics is no longer about coming from fourth position to emerge governor. He insisted that his task ahead of 2027 is to mobilise support for Tinubu’s re-election, not to intervene in local politics in the states. In a statement, yesterday, by his Senior Special Assistant on Public Communications and Social Media, Lere Olayinka, the minister said the Rainbow Coalition has nothing to do with the APC, describing the coalition as a platform for other political parties pleased with the good works of the President and supporting his re-election. Wike, who said he won’t be the one to help people win elections in their states, noted that “politics is local and those having problems in their states should resolve them instead of using the re-election of the President to whip up sentiments.” Wike pointed out that he never met with the APC before he and other members of the G5 supported the President in 2023, adding that for 2027, his support is for the president only. The minister said politics is no longer about coming from fourth position to be governor, but about genuinely mobilising support and winning elections from the polling units. Taking a direct swipe at Uzodinma’s home turf, he queried: “In Imo State under Governor Uzodinma, how did APC win two Senate seats in 2023, in an election held the same day with that of the President and APC had less than 15 per cent in the presidential election? Was it the rainbow coalition? Were the voters confused? “Was it the rainbow coalition that also made APC to win National Assembly elections in Ebonyi, Abia and Enugu states where the President did not have 10 per cent of the votes? “If in 2023, the voters in Imo, Abia, Enugu and Ebonyi voted APC in the senatorial election and voted another party in the presidential election, they won’t be confused in 2027, provided we all support the president genuinely this time.” The minister urged all stakeholders to put the presidential election first, saying “after the President must have been reelected, we can all go and face elections in our states. “What I said and stand for is that I will mobilise support for the re-election of the President. I never promised anyone that PDP will not field candidates to contest governorship, National Assembly and States House of Assembly elections. “Most importantly, the rainbow coalition has nothing to do with the APC. Rather, it is its way of mobilising support across political parties for Mr President, who has done well, to deserve a second term.’’ Wike is a force to reckon with, not reject , PDP tells APC govs Reacting yesterday, Peoples Democratic Party, PDP, hit back at the APC, governors over their reported rejection of Minister of the FCT, Nyesom Wike’s political support for President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, saying the former Rivers State governor remains a formidable force ahead of the 2027 elections. In a statement by the National Publicity Secretary, Jungudo Haruna Mohammed, the PDP said Wike has every constitutional and democratic right to choose whom he supports, arguing that his support for Tinubu did not mean he had abandoned the PDP or joined the APC. “Wike has every constitutional and democratic right to decide whom he supports politically. His support for President Tinubu is legitimate, and as a serving appointee of the President, there is nothing contradictory about supporting the President while maintaining his political identity and relationships within the PDP,” Jungudo said. The party said the APC governors had initially interpreted Wike’s support for Tinubu as an endorsement of the APC but were now confronted with the reality that the FCT minister could support the President while retaining his political identity and relationships within the PDP. It described as a ‘fundamental political miscalculation’ any attempt by the governors to dictate whether Wike should support or field candidates capable of challenging them and their preferred candidates in 2027. The PDP said every political party had the right to field candidates, adding that the reported position of the governors suggested that they were becoming increasingly anxious about facing strong opposition candidates at the polls. “If they have truly performed and retained the confidence of their people, they should welcome a contest and allow the electorate to decide,” the party said.
